India just banned bitchat. That should tell you everything you need to know about how powerful it is.

The app was pulled from both the App Store and Google Play in India after a demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Apple's reason: "it includes content that is illegal in India."

What content? It's a local mesh app that hops messages over Bluetooth between nearby phones. There's no data center full of messages for anyone to rifle through.

The timing says it all. The ban came right after authorities shut off mobile internet for 12 hours during a protest in Delhi. Bitchat was built for exactly that situation. No cell towers, no Wi-Fi, no accounts, no phone numbers, no central server to raid. Just phones talking to each other.

Here's the thing India's government doesn't seem to understand: bitchat is free and open source. They can pressure Apple and Google to stop distributing it. They can't make the code disappear.

Android users can grab the APK from GitHub and sideload it. The app even has a "Share BitChat" feature that sends itself to another phone over a local hotspot. No internet required. One person with the app can spread it to everyone around them.

We saw what this looks like in practice last year when Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica. Bitchat jumped to the second most downloaded app on the island. When banking and communications went down, people used bitcoin to move money and bitchat to talk to each other.

Download bitchat before you need it. App Store, Google Play, or the APK. You might not use it for a year. But when the towers go down or your government decides you shouldn't be able to talk to your neighbors, you'll be glad it's on your phone.

Get your family on it. Get your neighbors on it. This is a grassroots thing.

text:
Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Your app didn’t crash because of a bug. It crashed because the Indian government decided to block your backend.

Starting February 24th, https://t.co/cpotyIe5BS became unreachable across major Indian ISPs. Supabase later confirmed this was due to a ministry order. No prior notice. No public explanation. No transition window.

Jio. Airtel. ACT Fibernet. All started DNS-poisoning Supabase domains, redirecting API calls to a sinkhole IP. Every app running on Supabase in India (auth, database, edge functions, real-time) went dark for millions of users. Reports suggest Firebase Hosting is facing similar disruptions.

Thousands of startups, student projects, hackathon builds, production SaaS apps. Blocked. No “here’s 90 days to migrate.” Nothing.

Supabase had to publicly tag Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on X just to get someone to talk to them: “Supabase is used by millions of developers worldwide, and millions of users in India are currently unable to access our platform. Could we talk to someone in your team about this?”

Silence from MeitY. Silence from the Minister. Silence from every ISP.

Supabase is not a social media platform. It’s a PostgreSQL database wrapper with auth, storage, and APIs. Its users are engineers building software. There is no obvious legal or content-based reason to block it.

And this isn’t the first time. Medium blocked on Jio/Airtel in Oct 2025. Linktree blocked without explanation. BSNL blocked Dailymotion and Telegram links in Aug 2025. ACT Fibernet blocked TheMovieDB. Ubuntu mirrors and Cloudflare R2 hit before that.

Critical internet infrastructure keeps getting caught in opaque, unaccountable blocking orders. No public reasoning. No appeals process. No distinction between a piracy site and a developer tool.

The workaround? Switch DNS to 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. Use a VPN. Proxy backend traffic through custom domains so you’re not exposed to ISP blocks.

But think about what we’re saying. We’re telling Indian developers: “Your government might randomly block your backend, so architect around that.” That’s not a healthy ecosystem. That’s building on a minefield.

We talk about Digital India. Startup India. A $5 trillion economy. We want to compete globally in SaaS and AI.

But we’re blocking the tools our developers need to build. Without notice. Without reason. Without a plan.

India’s builders deserve better than this.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

India just banned bitchat. That should tell you everything you need to know about how powerful it is.

The app was pulled from both the App Store and Google Play in India after a demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Apple's reason: "it includes content that is illegal in India."

What content? It's a local mesh app that hops messages over Bluetooth between nearby phones. There's no data center full of messages for anyone to rifle through.

The timing says it all. The ban came right after authorities shut off mobile internet for 12 hours during a protest in Delhi. Bitchat was built for exactly that situation. No cell towers, no Wi-Fi, no accounts, no phone numbers, no central server to raid. Just phones talking to each other.

Here's the thing India's government doesn't seem to understand: bitchat is free and open source. They can pressure Apple and Google to stop distributing it. They can't make the code disappear.

Android users can grab the APK from GitHub and sideload it. The app even has a "Share BitChat" feature that sends itself to another phone over a local hotspot. No internet required. One person with the app can spread it to everyone around them.

We saw what this looks like in practice last year when Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica. Bitchat jumped to the second most downloaded app on the island. When banking and communications went down, people used bitcoin to move money and bitchat to talk to each other.

Download bitchat before you need it. App Store, Google Play, or the APK. You might not use it for a year. But when the towers go down or your government decides you shouldn't be able to talk to your neighbors, you'll be glad it's on your phone.

Get your family on it. Get your neighbors on it. This is a grassroots thing.

India banned Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat. The harder question is whether the ban can actually work.

The app runs over Bluetooth, with no SIM card or internet required.

Removing it from app stores does not erase copies already installed.

So can a government really kill technology designed to work when the internet disappears?

5. INDIAS PROBABLE SECURITY CONCERNS OVER STARLINK 

Whilst I am not privy to the security concerns of the Union Home Ministry and the CCCS (does it even exist anymore ?), some of the probable concerns are listed below.

a. The concern of whether India can maintain control over national security, communications, data, and spectrum while allowing a foreign-operated satellite network to provide internet across the country is a major worry.

b. National Security and Military Use 
-India will need to identify and investigate the misuse of satellite terminals.
-They will have to respond to lawful government orders to restrict service in specific locations or to specific users.
- They will have to prevent unauthorized communications from undermining military operations.
-Ensure that terminals and services are not being used to facilitate terrorism, smuggling, or other serious crimes.

This is not a hypothetical fear, as @Jairam_Ramesh   had correctly pointed out that Starlink equipment was recovered from Manipur in 2024, and also more recently  during a drug-related operation in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. 

c. Data Sovereignity and Protection 

The former MP @priyankac19 had raised some important questions in the Parliament on this aspect. 

India has to ensure that communications generated by Indian users remain subject to Indian law and that authorised agencies can obtain access when legally required.

The govt had replied on 7/8/2025 to Ms.Chaturvedi,  specifying security conditions for Starlink, including:
-Indian user traffic must not be routed through gateways outside India.
-Indian data must not be copied and decrypted outside India.
-Indian user traffic must not be mirrored to systems or servers abroad

https://t.co/2q54VIBAH3

d. Can India switch Starlink off during a crisis?
This is a major concern for India, because as we have seen, during times of local crisis or military insurgency, the Govt has switched off Internet!

Retaining operational control during a war, border confrontation, terrorist incident, or other emergency is critical.

e. Foreign ownership and strategic dependence

Starlink is operated by SpaceX, a US company owned & controlled by Elon Musk. This brings into question the  foreign ownership, corporate accountability, and dependence on infrastructure outside India's direct control.

In a Musk company, the govt has no clarity on who ultimately controls the service and its technical operations. Do ownership and investment structures meet India's foreign investment rules?

It's also important whether sensitive operational information could be accessed by foreign entities or enemy entities, and what remedies would India have if the operator failed to comply with its license conditions?

f. The risk of a foreign company becoming strategically indispensable

Starlink's network is via a global constellation and centralized service-management systems. India's reliance on one foreign provider could create strategic vulnerabilities if access were disrupted, commercial terms changed, or international relations deteriorated.

The issue of pricing and accessibility is also a concern but less pressing than the security concerns.

Dear Rahul Gandhi,

You say you have understood the RSS “inside out” for over a decade. Yet your understanding of its history seems to have skipped a few chapters.

Your great-grandfather’s government banned the RSS in 1948. Your grandmother’s government banned it during the Emergency in 1975. Another Congress-led government banned it in 1992.

Three bans. Three attempts to stop an organisation that began in 1925.

And what happened?

The bans were lifted. The RSS continued. And the organisation you keep declaring finished is still here.

If banning an organisation were enough to erase it, your family’s political legacy would have settled this question decades ago. Instead, you are still holding press conferences and writing posts about the same organisation.

The flooding occurred after a landslide blocked the flow of the Chumche Khola, leading to a sudden surge in the Budhi Gandaki River. Several areas, including Dobhan, Ghattikhola, Jagat and Salleri, reported extensive damage.

Authorities have urged residents living along the river and in low-lying areas to move to safer locations as water levels continue to rise. Nepal’s police, armed police force and local administration have been mobilised for rescue and relief operations, with helicopter deployment being prepared. The health emergency centre has also been activated.

text:
This Chandigarh court order suspending three Facebook pages over AI-generated political videos feels like a crack in the dam. I'm surprised by how quickly this is happening, and frankly, a little alarmed.

The court has directed Meta to take down pages like "Batale Di Rajneeti" and "Kachi Laan" until October 22, 2026, because of AI videos targeting politician Amandeep Jaintipur. These videos, which have already racked up 3 lakh views, paint him as an anti-social element and a drug dealer, with some even showing him making "woman-like gestures." I don't think you can get much more malicious than that.

What strikes me is that this is the third such order in the Chandigarh Tricity in just a year. The previous ones were for specific URLs, but this one goes after entire pages. It feels like a significant escalation, especially with Punjab elections looming in early 2027. My take is that the law is playing catch-up, and these court orders are a desperate attempt to plug a leak that’s already gushing.

The IT Rules from February 2026 require platforms to declare and label AI content. But the legal route to get stuff taken down still relies on court orders or specific government intimations. This whole process seems designed to create delays. I mean, suspending a whole page when the damage is done by specific videos? It’s a blunt instrument, and I can't help but wonder if it's effective or just a way to look like you're doing something.

#AI #Elections #Deepfakes

text:
Downloading Child Pornography is an Offence?

➡️ According to IT Act, 2000 - Downloading sexually explicit material pertaining to #children is an #offence.

➡️ Also, The National Crime Records Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs, and the American National Center for Missing & Exploited Children prosecute those who upload child sexual abuse materials (#CSAM).

➡️ The #POCSO Act punishes storage or possession of child pornographic material only if it is done with intent to share, transmit, display, distribute, or for commercial purpose.

#UPSC Aspirants must understand #ITAct, 2000 fully to do justice to questions from this domain.

Read this post to know everything about IT ACT, 2000 👇

1️⃣ What is IT Act?
▪️ The Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) is the primary law in India governing Information Technology (IT) and its applications. It was enacted to:
Facilitate electronic #commerce: Provide legal recognition for electronic transactions and digital signatures.
▪️ Combat cybercrime: Define and penalise various cyber offences like #hacking, data #theft, and online fraud.
▪️ Promote electronic governance: Enable government agencies to deliver services electronically.

2️⃣ Why is IT act required?
▪️ With the increasing reliance on technology in everyday life, a legal framework was needed to address issues like #online fraud, security threats, and #data privacy.

3️⃣ Ministries involved
▪️ Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (#MeitY): Responsible for formulating and implementing IT policies, including the IT Act.
▪️ Ministry of Home Affairs (#MHA): Primarily involved in cybercrime investigation and enforcement.
▪️ Ministry of Law and Justice: Involved in drafting and reviewing amendments to the IT Act.

4️⃣ Important Amendments:
▪️ IT Amendment Act, 2002: Introduced sections dealing with cyber terrorism and obscenity in electronic form.

▪️ IT Amendment Act, 2008: Strengthened cybercrime provisions, introduced data protection obligations, and established the Cyber Appellate Tribunal.
- Strengthened cybercrime provisions: Added new offences like identity theft, data theft, and online fraud. Increased penalties for existing offences.
- Data protection obligations: Introduced the requirement for companies to implement reasonable security practices to protect personal data. This was a first step towards a comprehensive data protection framework, which is still under development.
- Established the Cyber Appellate #Tribunal: Created a dedicated tribunal for handling appeals against orders passed by adjudicating officers under the IT Act.

▪️ IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021:
- These rules, notified under the IT Act, impose various obligations on social media platforms and other online intermediaries, including takedown requests, content moderation, and user verification.
- The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and #DigitalMedia #Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, released in 2021, regulates social media, digital media, and #OTT platforms.
- IT Rules (2021) mandate social media platforms to exercise greater diligence with respect to the content on their platforms.
- The intermediary shall prominently publish on its website, mobile based application or both, as the case may be, the rules and regulations, privacy policy and user agreement for access or usage of its computer resource by any person
- The intermediary shall, as soon as possible, but not later than seventy two hours of the receipt of an order, provide information under its control or possession, or assistance to the Government agency which is lawfully authorised for investigative or protective or cyber security activities, for the purposes of verification of identity, or for the prevention, detection, investigation, or prosecution, of offences under any law for the time being in force, or for cyber security incidents
- The intermediary shall report cyber security incidents and share related information with the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team in accordance with the policies and procedures
- The intermediary shall, within twenty-four hours from the receipt of a complaint made by an individual or any person on his behalf under this sub-rule, in relation to any content which is prima facie in the nature of any material which exposes the private area of such individual, shows such individual in full or partial nudity or shows or depicts such individual in any sexual act or conduct, or is in the nature of impersonation in an electronic form, including artificially morphed images of such individual, take all reasonable and practicable measures to remove or disable access to such content which is hosted, stored, published or transmitted by it
- Appoint a Chief Compliance Officer who shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with the Act and rules
- Appoint a nodal contact person for 24x7 coordination with law enforcement agencies and officers to ensure #compliance to their orders or requisitions made in accordance with the provisions of law or #rules
- Publish periodic compliance report every month mentioning the details of complaints received and action taken thereon
- OTT platforms must adhere to the following rules:
🚩Content classification
🚩Age ratings
🚩Self-regulation
🚩Content removal and compliance officers
🚩Grievance redressal mechanisms
🚩The government has the authority to block content in exceptional cases.

▪️ IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2023:

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

Ruby Mills was incorporated in 1917. The coming annual general meeting is its 110th, so shareholder meetings here predate microphones as standard equipment.

By its own description the company is in textiles and real estate. That pairing is the arithmetic of an old Bombay mill rather than a change of plan. A mill starts with looms and accumulates land. The land in Dadar ends up as interesting to the accounts department as the looms in Khopoli. The company's Development Agreement covered part of its vacant mill land at Dadar. Construction costs were reimbursed by the developer, and the consideration was set as a specified percentage of the developer's revenue. A renewed Occupation Certificate for The Ruby Tower, including the upper floors, was obtained in the 2021-22 financial year. Premium was paid to the Mumbai municipal corporation and to the State Government.

Recent filings have been busier than the minute books of 1917 were built for. In August 2026 the company disclosed the sale of 33rd-floor commercial premises in The Ruby, along with car parking spaces. The buyer was Torrent Pharmaceuticals and the consideration was ₹124.08 crore. In September 2025 it executed a loan agreement of ₹13.75 crore. It also invested ₹1.65 crore for 19.99% of Jambavati LLP, a limited liability partnership. In March 2026 it incorporated Ruby GreenTech T Private Limited and Ruby GreenTech K Private Limited, both wholly owned. Zydus Wellness is the consumer arm of the Zydus group. It develops, makes, markets and distributes health and wellness products, running the whole chain itself. Sugar Free, Everyuth and Nutralite are the founding trio. Glucon-D, Complan and Nycil arrived with the Heinz India acquisition in 2019.

The buying did not stop there. Carnation Nutra came in 2020. Naturell (India) Private Limited, which owns the RiteBite Max Protein range of bars, cookies and chips, followed on 30 October 2024. The price was ₹390 crore, of which ₹369 crore was paid upfront. The remaining ₹21 crore was tied to earnouts, payments that depend on later performance. The whole sum was funded in cash. Naturell was then voluntarily wound up on a going-concern basis. Its entire business undertaking passed into the parent with effect from 20 September 2025.

The largest step came on 29 August 2025. Wholly-owned subsidiary Alidac UK Limited completed the purchase of Comfort Click Limited for GBP 239 million. A profit-ticker payment of GBP 2.64 million came on top. A GBP 240 million bridge loan funded the deal at first. Comfort Click reported revenue of GBP 134 million in its 2025 financial year. The purchase price allocation is still provisional. It will be finalised within the measurement period allowed by Ind AS 103, the accounting rule for takeovers.

The 2019 Heinz deal came with a capital restructure. The company raised ₹1,000 crore through a QIP and a preferential issue, both share sales to large institutions. It also repurchased ₹1,500 crore of non-convertible debentures, a form of company borrowing. In September 2025 the face value of the equity was split from ₹10 to ₹2.

The legal residue of the Heinz vintage is still live. DGGI Surat, the GST authority's investigation arm, confirmed a demand of ₹56.33 crore on Zydus Wellness Products Limited in September 2025. The Gujarat High Court granted interim relief in January 2026. The company states the liability is indemnified by Heinz Italia. A separate GST order in March 2026 imposed a penalty of ₹0.63 crore plus interest, covering 2019-20 and 2020-21.

The silent bottleneck of the AI boom. And why India is quietly becoming the world's answer.

A hyperscale data centre operator in the US had everything ready last year.

Chips. Land. Permits. Engineers.

And then they hit the one thing they could not solve by writing a cheque.

They could not get the transformers.

The waiting list for large power transformers in the US is now 2 to 3 years. Not weeks. Years.

Every data centre, every ageing utility, every solar farm, every EV charging hub needs them. All are being told to wait.

For 30 years, nobody built transformer capacity.
The sector was unglamorous and low-margin. Western manufacturers consolidated or exited.

Then AI, EVs and renewables arrived all at once. This quiet corner of the industrial world became the chokepoint of the modern economy.

Here is where it gets interesting for an Indian investor.
While the world ignored transformers, India quietly built capability.

We now have manufacturers who meet Western voltage specifications, win international orders, and ship at a cost no Western plant can match.

India has committed over ₹9 lakh crore of transmission capex through 2032.

Add the 500 GW renewable target.
Add the data centre buildout.
Add EV charging infrastructure.
Add a replacement cycle on our own installed base.

The demand curve looks like a hockey stick.

Then add the export layer, where Indian manufacturers are now winning global orders at the best margins they have ever earned.

India's transformer market itself is projected to grow from $3.8 billion in 2026 to $8 billion by 2035.
This is a full value chain opportunity.

Core manufacturers:
TARIL, Shilchar Technologies, Voltamp Danish Power, Supreme Power, CG Power, Hitachi Energy India, Vilas Transcore, Raksan Transformer etc

Critical inputs:
CRGO electrical steel (the biggest bottleneck), copper (Hindustan Copper, Hindalco), transformer oil (Apar, Savita Oil), insulators (Quality Power, Aditya Birla Insulators).

Adjacent beneficiaries:
Skipper, KEC International, Kalpataru (EPC).
Siemens, ABB, Schneider, L&T (switchgear).
Polycab, KEI, Finolex (cables).

The demand is written into policy documents. The supply bottleneck is global. The order books are already visible.

Solar. EVs. AI. Data centres. Manufacturing.

Every one of them sits downstream of the transformer.
The next decade of India's growth story runs through its grid.

Kotak sec write up:

*Polycab India was placed under the IBC framework because the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Ahmedabad Bench, admitted an insolvency petition against the company on October 7, 2026, initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).*
Details Behind the Admission
 The Petitioner: The insolvency plea was filed under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) by an operational creditor, Asier Metals Private Limited.
 Claim Amount: The dispute involves an alleged unpaid operational debt of approximately ₹2.79 crore.
 Automatic Exchange Mechanism: Under SEBI and stock exchange surveillance guidelines, the moment an NCLT bench officially admits an insolvency plea against a listed entity, the exchange is required to automatically shift the scrip into the IBC Surveillance Framework. This triggers mandatory risk controls, including removal from the F&O segment, 100% margin requirements, and eventual price-band curbs.
The Company’s Stand
 Commercial Dispute: Polycab has stated that the ₹2.79 crore claim is a pre-existing commercial dispute involving credit notes, ledger reconciliation, and demurrage adjustments rather than financial distress.
 Financial Position: The disputed amount is immaterial relative to Polycab's balance sheet (the company holds over ₹4,000 crore in cash/liquid balances and a net worth exceeding ₹11,000 crore).
 Legal Recourse: Polycab immediately filed an appeal before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) seeking a stay/quashing of the NCLT order.
If the NCLAT grants an interim stay or dismisses the CIRP admission order, Polycab can approach the stock exchanges to review and potentially revoke the IBC surveillance measures.

*Polycab could be at risk of MSCI deletion*: MSCI's India Ineligible Alert Board (IAB) policy explicitly includes India's Enhanced Surveillance Measure (ESM) and Insolvency Resolution Process frameworks on the Bombay Stock Exchange and National Stock Exchange.

Under that policy:
Securities included on the IAB are excluded from the MSCI Equity Universe.
Existing MSCI constituents entering the IAB are deleted on the last business day of the month, with at least two full business days' notice.
Such securities cannot be added back to MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes for 12 months following deletion.

The 11th National Annual Stakeholders’ Consultation named “A Decade of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015: Progress, Challenges and Priorities for the Next Decade” was held on October 10–11 at the Supreme Court Auditorium, New Delhi, organised by the Supreme Court of India, UNICEF India and the Union Ministry of Women and Child Development. 

Odisha was represented by Dr. Mrinalini Darswal, IAS, Commissioner-Cum-Secretary Women & Child Development Dept. 

The consultation brought together judicial experts, senior officials and child rights stakeholders to discuss progress and priorities in child protection and juvenile justice.

Odisha showcased its achievements in implementing the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, re-affirming its commitment to child-centred care, protection, rehabilitation and empowerment.

Key achievements include:
🔹 Family-Based Care: Sponsorship support increased from 689 children in 2016 to 5,550 in 2026, while children in Child Care Institutions declined from 17,411 to 7,289.
🔹 Support for Vulnerable Children: Initiatives such as Ashirbad, Jashoda and Kalika provide financial assistance, long-term support and safe childcare.
🔹 Empowerment: Education, life skills, vocational training, sports and cultural activities help children build confidence and prepare for independent futures.
🔹 Child-Friendly Justice: Improved infrastructure, judicial oversight, rescue and restoration initiatives, and digital safety programmes strengthen child protection systems.

Speaking at the consultation, Dr. Mrinalini Darswal, IAS, Commissioner-cum-Secretary, Department of Women & Child Development, Government of Odisha, emphasised:

“Institutional care remains necessary for children who need it, but it should not become the default. Our systems increasingly aim to support children safely within families and communities wherever possible.”

Odisha’s experience highlights that effective child protection requires strong families and communities, rehabilitation and opportunities for every child to thrive.
Every child deserves a family, protection, and a future filled with dignity, opportunity and hope.

କିଶୋର ନ୍ୟାୟ ଅଧିନିୟମ, ୨୦୧୫ର ଏକ ଦଶନ୍ଧି: ପ୍ରଗତି, ଆହ୍ୱାନ ଏବଂ ଆଗାମୀ ଦଶନ୍ଧି ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରାଥମିକତା ନାମରେ    ୧୧ତମ ଜାତୀୟ ବାର୍ଷିକ ଅଂଶୀଦାର ସମ୍ମିଳନୀ, ଅକ୍ଟୋବର ୧୦-୧୧ ତାରିଖରେ ନୂଆଦିଲ୍ଲୀର ସୁପ୍ରିମକୋର୍ଟ ଅଡିଟୋରିୟମରେ ଅନୁଷ୍ଠିତ ହୋଇଥିଲା। ଏହାକୁ ଭାରତର ସୁପ୍ରିମକୋର୍ଟ, ୟୁନିସେଫ୍ ଇଣ୍ଡିଆ ଏବଂ କେନ୍ଦ୍ର ମହିଳା ଓ ଶିଶୁ ବିକାଶ ମନ୍ତ୍ରଣାଳୟ ମିଳିତଭାବେ ଆୟୋଜନ କରିଥିଲେ । 

ଓଡ଼ିଶା ପ୍ରତିନିଧି ଭାବରେ ମହିଳା ଓ ଶିଶୁ ବିକାଶ ବିଭାଗର କମିଶନର-ତଥା-ସଚିବ ଡ. ମୃଣାଳିନୀ ଦର୍ଶୱାଲ, ଆଇ.ଏ.ଏସ୍. ଅଂଶଗ୍ରହଣ କରିଥିଲେ। ଏହି ସମ୍ମିଳନୀରେ ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ଏବଂ କିଶୋର ନ୍ୟାୟ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରେ ପ୍ରଗତି ଏବଂ ପ୍ରାଥମିକତା ଉପରେ ଆଲୋଚନା କରିବା ପାଇଁ ନ୍ୟାୟିକ ବିଶେଷଜ୍ଞ, ବରିଷ୍ଠ ଅଧିକାରୀ ଏବଂ ଶିଶୁ ଅଧିକାର ଅଂଶୀଦାରମାନେ ଏକତ୍ରିତ ହୋଇଥିଲେ। କିଶୋର ନ୍ୟାୟ (ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କର ଯତ୍ନ ଏବଂ ସୁରକ୍ଷା) ଅଧିନିୟମ, ୨୦୧୫ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟକାରୀ କରିବାରେ ଓଡ଼ିଶା ନିଜର ସଫଳତା ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶନ କରିଥିଲା ଏବଂ ଶିଶୁ-କୈନ୍ଦ୍ରିକ ଯତ୍ନ, ସୁରକ୍ଷା, ପୁନର୍ବାସ ଏବଂ ସଶକ୍ତିକରଣ ପ୍ରତି ଏହାର ପ୍ରତିବଦ୍ଧତାକୁ ପୁନଃପ୍ରକାଶ କରିଥିଲା।

ଓଡ଼ିଶାର ପ୍ରମୁଖ ସଫଳତାଗୁଡ଼ିକ ହେଲା:
• ପାରିବାରିକ ଯତ୍ନ: ପ୍ରାୟୋଜକ ସହାୟତା ୨୦୧୬ରେ ୬୮୯ ଜଣ ଶିଶୁରୁ ବୃଦ୍ଧି ପାଇ ୨୦୨୬ରେ ୫,୫୫୦ ଜଣରେ ପହଞ୍ଚିଛି, ଯେତେବେଳେ କି ଶିଶୁ ଯତ୍ନ ଅନୁଷ୍ଠାନଗୁଡ଼ିକରେ ଥିବା ଶିଶୁଙ୍କ ସଂଖ୍ୟା ୧୭,୪୧୧ ରୁ କମି ୭,୨୮୯କୁ ଖସିଆସିଛି।
• ଅସୁରକ୍ଷିତ ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କୁ ସହାୟତା: 'ଆଶୀର୍ବାଦ', 'ଯଶୋଦା' ଏବଂ 'କଳିକା' ଭଳି ପଦକ୍ଷେପଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଆର୍ଥିକ ସହାୟତା, ଦୀର୍ଘକାଳୀନ ସହଯୋଗ ଏବଂ ନିରାପଦ ଶିଶୁ ଯତ୍ନ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରୁଛି।
• ସଶକ୍ତିକରଣ: ଶିକ୍ଷା, ଜୀବନ କୌଶଳ, ବୃତ୍ତିଗତ ପ୍ରଶିକ୍ଷଣ, କ୍ରୀଡ଼ା ଏବଂ ସାଂସ୍କୃତିକ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟକ୍ରମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କୁ ଆତ୍ମବିଶ୍ୱାସ ବଢ଼ାଇବା ଏବଂ ସ୍ୱାଧୀନ ଭବିଷ୍ୟତ ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତ ହେବାରେ ସାହାଯ୍ୟ କରୁଛି।
• ଶିଶୁ-ଅନୁକୂଳ ନ୍ୟାୟ: ଉନ୍ନତ ଭିତ୍ତିଭୂମି, ଆଇନଗତ ତଦାରଖ, ଉଦ୍ଧାର ଓ ପୁନରୁଦ୍ଧାର ପଦକ୍ଷେପ ଏବଂ ଡିଜିଟାଲ୍ ସୁରକ୍ଷା କାର୍ଯ୍ୟକ୍ରମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥାକୁ ମଜଭୁତ କରୁଛି।

ସମ୍ମିଳନୀରେ ମତାମତ ରଖି ଓଡ଼ିଶା ସରକାରଙ୍କ ମହିଳା ଓ ଶିଶୁ ବିକାଶ ବିଭାଗର କମିଶନର-ତଥା-ସଚିବ ଡ. ମୃଣାଳିନୀ ଦର୍ଶୱାଲ ଗୁରୁତ୍ୱାରୋପ କରି କହିଥିଲେ "ଯେଉଁ ଶିଶୁମାନଙ୍କୁ ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ଅନୁଷ୍ଠାନଗତ ଯତ୍ନ ଆବଶ୍ୟକ, ସେମାନଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ ଏହା ଜରୁରୀ ହୋଇପାରେ , କିନ୍ତୁ ଏହା ସବୁବେଳେ ପ୍ରାଥମିକ ବିକଳ୍ପ ହେବା ଉଚିତ୍ ନାହିଁ। ଆମର ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥାଗୁଡ଼ିକ କ୍ରମଶଃ ଏହି ଦିଗରେ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟ କରୁଛି ଯେଉଁଠାରେ ସମ୍ଭବ ଶିଶୁମାନେ ପରିବାର ଏବଂ ସମାଜ ମଧ୍ୟରେ ନିରାପଦରେ ରହି ସହାୟତା ପାଇପାରିବେ।"
ଓଡ଼ିଶାର ଏହି ଅନୁଭୂତି ପ୍ରମାଣ କରେ ଯେ ପ୍ରଭାବଶାଳୀ ଶିଶୁ ସୁରକ୍ଷା ପାଇଁ ଦୃଢ଼ ପରିବାର ଓ ସମାଜ, ପୁନର୍ବାସ ଏବଂ ପ୍ରତ୍ୟେକ ଶିଶୁର ବିକାଶ ପାଇଁ ସୁଯୋଗ ଏକାନ୍ତ ଆବଶ୍ୟକ ।

The Union Government and Delhi Police have told Delhi High Court X is liable to lose its safe harbour protection in India because it failed to act against Rana Ayyub’s offensive tweets about Hindu deities and Savarkar.

Here’s @barandbench report on what transpired in court:

The Government has said that the police had issued notices in September 2025 and December 2025, requesting X to take down Ayyub’s posts. The Government said that in January 2025, a trial court ordered registration of an FIR against Ayyub over these posts.

The police notices and trial court order constitute “actual knowledge” under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, triggering a statutory obligation on X to act expeditiously and remove such unlawful content, the High Court has been told.

It added that as X failed to act despite “actual knowledge” the safe harbour protection available to it is liable to be withdrawn.

Notably, the High Court had on April 8, 2026 observed that these tweets (made between 2013-2017) were derogatory and communal. 

After the hearing, the Delhi Police sent a request to MEITY to block the content and the request is under consideration, the Court has been told.

Meanwhile, X has also filed a response in the High Court and said that the petition should be directed against Rana Ayyub (the uploader of the content) and not X. 

It also also directions to Delhi Police to follow the  2009 Blocking Rules and issue a blocking order under Section 69A of the IT Act.

Rana Ayyub's lawyers told the Court today that the writ petition was not maintainable. 

The HC has granted Ayyub two weeks time to file a reply in the case, including on the issue of maintainability.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.
