INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨 #FACTCHECK: Nigel Farage on Burnham, Russia and Brexit

‘Mirror, mirror, on the wall, whose claims stand up after all?’

I’m a retired academic, media literate, and equipped with critical thinking skills, so I have time to do this quickly and accurately.

Earlier today, Nigel Farage called Prime Minister Andy Burnham “a liar” over his claim that Russia interfered in the 2016 EU referendum. Here is how Farage’s statements hold up against the record.

In an interview with The Rest Is Politics  podcast, released on 12 October but widely reported the day before, Burnham said that on taking office in July he asked whether Russia had interfered in the 2016 referendum, and was given “the clear answer that yes there was.” He did not say how Russia interfered and did not publish any evidence.

This morning, Farage held a press conference in Dover, Kent, to launch Reform UK’s asylum plans. LBC’s Emma Corr asked whether Burnham’s claim tainted the result, and how Farage felt about having potentially benefited from possible Russian interference. He later repeated several of his claims in an interview with GB News.

The exchange between Corr and Farage is available on YouTube from 1:00:07: https://t.co/zJMuAlHXdx

1. “The prime minister is a liar. Yes, a liar.”

Verdict: Unsupported.

Lying means knowingly saying something false. Burnham reported advice he says he received on entering No 10. That advice has not been made public, so his claim is unverified, and critics are entitled to say so. Nothing Farage cited shows that Burnham knew it to be untrue. At most, Farage offered evidence that the claim is unproven.

2. “Boris Johnson, when he became foreign secretary, one of the first questions he asked was, ‘Was there seen to be Russian interference in the referendum campaign?’ And the answer was no.”

Verdict: Misleading.

I could find no public record of this exchange. Johnson’s recorded public position was more qualified. In Moscow in December 2017, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said Johnson had confirmed Russia had not interfered in the referendum. Johnson interrupted him: “Not successfully.” He went on to say that Russian attempts to interfere in British elections and the referendum, whatever they may have been, had not succeeded. His position was that attempts may have been made and had failed, which is a different claim from “no”.

The premise that anyone checked is also doubtful. Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) published its Russia Report in July 2020. It found that the government “had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference” in UK democratic processes. It called for an intelligence assessment of the referendum, and the government refused.

In 2019, BuzzFeed reported two anonymous sources saying British intelligence had found no evidence of Russian meddling in the referendum. That claim was unverified, and the ISC’s report the following year said the government had not sought such evidence.

3. Stephen Doughty “rowed it back and said even if there was some, it made no difference.”

Verdict: Misrepresents the minister.

Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, did narrow Burnham’s claim during Monday morning’s broadcast interviews. He told LBC that Russia had attempted to interfere in the vote but had not succeeded, and made the same point to Sky News. He also said Burnham had been making a broader point about Russian attempts to interfere in democratic events in the UK and across Europe.

On the @BBC Today programme, which Farage named, Doughty spoke of Russian attempts to interfere in a range of democratic processes. He cited the jailing of former Reform UK Wales leader Nathan Gill for taking bribes to promote pro-Kremlin narratives.

Farage’s summary distorts this. “Even if there was some” turns Doughty’s acknowledgement of attempts into a hypothetical. Farage followed it with the words “There was no Russian interference,” and in his later GB News interview (see 10) he attributed that denial to Doughty himself. I found no report of Doughty’s interviews containing those words, or anything to that effect. Doughty said Russia tried to interfere.

4. “There was no Russian interference… And the Russia hoax has run all the way through this.”

Verdict: Not supported by the evidence.

No official finding says there was no interference. The government’s position since 2020 has been narrower: “We have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU Referendum.” The ISC noted open-source studies pointing to anti-EU content on the Russian state outlets RT and Sputnik, and to the use of bots and trolls, as evidence of attempts to influence the campaign. It criticised the government for not investigating.

The defensible position is that attempts at influence were plausibly documented, their effect was never assessed, and no public evidence shows they changed the result. “No interference” and “hoax” both go well beyond that. The same standard applies to Burnham, whose “clear answer” rests on advice the public has not seen.

5. Arron Banks “was severely libelled over this. But in the end … [he] won in the high court.”

Verdict: False.

Banks sued the journalist Carole Cadwalladr over a 2019 TED Talk and a tweet. He lost in the High Court in June 2022, where the judge held that Cadwalladr’s public interest defence covered the talk. In February 2023, the Court of Appeal found partly in his favour, on one of his three grounds of appeal. It ruled that the defence lapsed for the talk’s continued publication after 29 April 2020, the date of an Electoral Commission statement clearing Banks. It upheld the dismissal of his claim over the tweet. Cadwalladr was ordered to pay £35,000 in damages and 60% of Banks’s High Court costs.

The case also had no bearing on whether Russia interfered in the referendum. It concerned Cadwalladr’s statement about Banks and “his covert relationship with the Russian Government.”

6. “I don’t think our growth figures are anything to write home about. But … they’re a damn sight better than France and Germany and Italy.”

Verdict: Accurate for this year, but selective over the longer term, and beside the point.

On current figures Farage has a case. In the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 0.5%, against 0.3% in Germany and zero in France. The IMF’s July forecasts put the UK third in the G7 for 2026, at 1%, behind the US (2.3%) and Canada (1.1%). That is ahead of Germany (0.7%), France and Japan (both 0.6%) and Italy (0.5%). The OECD’s September forecasts placed the UK joint second in the G7, level with Germany at 1.1%.

The longer view is less flattering. Between the end of 2019 and the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 6.2%, behind the eurozone as a whole (7.6%) and far behind the US (15.6%), though well ahead of Germany (1.9%, the lowest in the G7).

By naming France, Germany and Italy, Farage compared the UK with three of Europe’s weaker performers, while the eurozone overall has grown faster since the pandemic. Headline growth has also been flattered by rapid population growth. In late 2024, the Resolution Foundation found UK GDP per head still below its end-2019 level, although per-head growth picked up to 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026.

More importantly, none of these comparisons answers Burnham’s claim. Whether Brexit has done “more harm than good” depends on how the UK compares with a UK that stayed in the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) assumes Brexit will leave UK trade around 15% lower in the long run, and potential productivity around 4% lower, than if the UK had remained. In 2024 it said these assumptions appeared “broadly on track.”

Some economists, including Julian Jessop, a former chief economist and head of the Brexit unit at the free-market Institute of Economic Affairs, dispute these estimates.

Even so, the official forecaster’s central view is that Brexit carries a long-run cost, and growth rankings, whether flattering or not, do not settle the question.

7. “If you even look at trade numbers, the increase in trade since Brexit…”

Verdict: Partly accurate, but selective.

Total UK exports have grown since the referendum. Briefings for Britain, a pro-Brexit research group using ONS data, puts total exports in 2025 at 5% above 2019 in real terms. That growth has come from services. The House of Commons Library reports that UK services exports to the EU were 28% above their 2019 level in real terms in 2025. However, goods exports to the EU were 14% below it, having fallen in real terms in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Not all of that fall is due to Brexit, but post-Brexit barriers fall mainly on goods, and goods trade with the EU is where the decline shows. The overall total obscures it.

8. Brexit has brought “some level of inconvenience… showing a passport, filling in a form,” amounting to “mild inconveniences.”

Verdict: Understatement.

Farage conceded there was more inconvenience “for people like Alcaline,” a Kent road haulage firm based near Hythe, but described it as “showing a passport, filling in a form.” The evidence suggests that undersells the effect, particularly for firms moving goods across the Channel.

In March 2024 the OBR reported that UK goods trade was around 10% below 2019 levels and growing well behind other advanced economies, while services trade had grown more strongly than in the rest of the G7. The OBR attributed the gap partly to post-Brexit barriers falling mainly on goods.

Brexit is not the only cause of the 14% real-terms fall in goods exports to the EU, but official forecasters attribute part of it to post-Brexit trade barriers, which go well beyond passports and forms. Farage’s answer also merges two separate issues: control of migration, and the trade frictions that come from leaving the single market and customs union.

9. Burnham is “looking forward to sitting down with Marine Le Pen or the AfD”

Verdict: Speculation, contrary to the record.

Farage offered no basis for this. In the interview that prompted the row, Burnham cited the German chancellor’s view that the AfD were linked to, and possibly funded by, Russia. He presented the party as a threat to European democracy.

10. The GB News version

Verdict: False.

In an interview with GB News later that day, Farage said Doughty, “being interviewed on the BBC this morning, disavowed it and said no, there was no Russian interference, it didn’t affect anything.” The “even if there was some” qualification had gone, leaving a flat denial attributed to the minister. Doughty’s reported position was that Russia attempted to interfere but did not succeed, which confirms attempted interference.

Farage also presented Johnson and Doughty together as evidence that “both Labour and Conservative camps” reject Burnham’s claim. Neither man said there was no interference. Johnson’s recorded words in 2017 were “Not successfully.” Doughty said Russia had tried and failed. What both rejected was the narrower claim that interference succeeded, which is also the extent of the official government position since 2020.

Conclusion

Farage’s sharpest claims are his weakest. Nothing presented shows that Burnham lied.

Johnson’s record says “not successfully” rather than “no”. The minister Farage cited acknowledged Russian attempts. In Dover, Farage turned that acknowledgement into a hypothetical, and on GB News into a flat denial. Banks did not win in the High Court.

Farage is on firmer ground on recent growth rankings and on total exports, though neither settles whether Brexit has helped or harmed the UK, and goods trade with the EU tells a different story.

Burnham, for his part, has made a significant claim without publishing the evidence behind it. The assessment the ISC recommended six years ago would serve the public better than either man’s certainty.

Finally, it is worth measuring Farage by his own yardstick. Farage called the British prime minister a liar. 

The evidence he offered went only to whether Burnham was wrong, not to whether he knew it. If being wrong, or being unable to prove a claim, is enough to make someone a liar, the same test can be applied to Farage.

By that standard, his answer in Dover contained five “lies”: that Johnson was told there was no interference; that Doughty conceded only that any interference “made no difference”; that there was no Russian interference; that the affair was a “hoax”; and that Arron Banks “won in the high court.”

On GB News he added a sixth, that “both Labour and Conservative camps” deny any interference, and repeated three of the others.

That makes six distinct claims, and nine in all, across two appearances in a single day. The row began over one claim by Burnham.

The fairer test, and the one this fact check applies, is that lying requires knowing a statement to be false. By that measure, nobody can say Farage lied, any more than he can say it of Burnham.

But on the evidence, Burnham’s claim remains unproven, while at least one of Farage’s, about his friend’s libel case, is plainly false on the public record.

Emerald Heights International School, Indore, and its Director (Academics), Siddharth Singh Girnar, have filed an Article 32 PIL contending that children are "routinely exposed to social-media platforms that are not designed or operated as child-safe environments."

The plea proposes a graded model: no accounts below 13; ages 13 to 16 only with the "verifiable consent and supervision of the parent or guardian"; and ages 16 to 18 subject to data protection and safeguards against harmful content.

The petitioners call this "far less intrusive than a complete prohibition."

#SupremeCourt #SocialMedia #ChildSafety #PIL

🚨 "There is no rational basis for exempting social media platforms from age verification…"

The Indore school's PIL in the Supreme Court points out that OTT platforms must verify age before showing adult content and online games are subject to age verification. 

Yet, it says: "A child cannot lawfully buy liquor, tobacco or acid, however, the same child can open a social media account without any verification and access similar or worse content, and can be contacted by any stranger."

Relying on an NCPCR study of 2021, the petition states that "37.8% of 10-year-old children surveyed had Facebook accounts" and alleges that platforms "have chosen not to act, because more users mean more revenue for them."

#SupremeCourt #Article14 #NCPCR #SocialMedia

🚨 "The protection therefore remains on paper."

The social media PIL in the Supreme Court contends that Section 9 of the DPDP Act, 2023, which requires verifiable parental consent and prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children, is yet to be brought into force.

As the child-related provisions take effect only in May 2027, the petition says the protection "will thus have remained inoperative for almost four years."

Distinguishing Zep Foundation (2025), where the Court declined to impose a ban as a policy matter, it says: "More than seventeen months have since passed without any framework being put in place."

The petitioners say they do not ask the Court "to frame the policy" and seek enforcement of existing law and a time-bound decision by the Government.

Garima Singh of Desh Ki Garima raises a serious contradiction that every citizen should examine.

India’s response to the United Nations human rights office defended the country’s democratic institutions, independent judiciary, free media and constitutional protection for peaceful assembly. Yet, during the recent Delhi protests, journalists and protesters reported detention, rough handling and the seizure of recording equipment.

According to the video, journalist Anil Shukla’s camera was seized by people alleged to be Delhi Police personnel and was not returned. This specific allegation demands verification and an official explanation.

THE QUESTION IS SIMPLE: IF INDIA’S INSTITUTIONS PROTECT PRESS FREEDOM, WHY ARE JOURNALISTS REPORTING THAT THEY WERE PREVENTED FROM DOING THEIR JOB?

This is not merely a political argument. On 10 October, the United Nations human rights office expressed concern over reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, civil-society members, lawyers and journalists. On 11 October, India rejected those concerns as unwarranted interference in its internal affairs.

Human Rights Watch, in its statement dated 13 October 2026, also reported allegations of excessive force, arbitrary detention and the seizure of journalists’ phones and equipment during the protests. These reports call for transparent investigation and accountability—not blanket dismissal or uncritical acceptance of every allegation.

A DEMOCRACY MUST BE JUDGED BY ITS CONDUCT, NOT ONLY BY ITS OFFICIAL STATEMENTS.

The Constitution protects freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19(1)(b), subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions.

Police may enforce lawful restrictions, but journalists must not be obstructed or have their equipment unlawfully seized merely because they document events that authorities find uncomfortable. Any seizure or detention must have a lawful basis and remain open to scrutiny.

We demand:

• A transparent account of every journalist detained during the protests.

• An explanation of the reported seizure of Anil Shukla’s camera, including its present whereabouts and the legal grounds for the action.

• An independent investigation into allegations of assault, intimidation and obstruction of journalists.

• Accountability wherever misconduct is established.

• Respect for peaceful protest, press freedom and the constitutional rights of every citizen.

India cannot claim democratic credibility internationally while leaving credible allegations of violations at home unanswered. Patriotism does not mean shielding institutions from scrutiny. It means demanding that they honour the Constitution.

LET THE FACTS BE EXAMINED. LET THE PRESS REPORT FREELY. LET PEACEFUL CITIZENS EXERCISE THEIR CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS.

IFF condemns journalist’s detention and the seizure of their phones during the Delhi protests

New Delhi, 12 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the detention of journalists and the seizure of their' phones by the Delhi Police during the protests of 10 and 11 October 2026. The protests, sought the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. According to a report in Newslaundry, the police took three official phones from its reporters and an intern on 10 October. BOOM lost contact with its reporter Jagriti Trisha after her phone was taken, and Indian Express Hindi said its journalist Siya's phone was snatched on 11 October. Scroll's Shoaib Daniyal says he was pressured to delete videos he recorded inside a police bus.

Section 106 of the BNSS allows the police to seize property only in connection with a suspected offence, and Section 105 requires every seizure to be video recorded and the recording sent to a Magistrate. No provision, seizure memo or recording has been made public, and it is not known whether the phones were unlocked or their data copied. A reporter's phone holds unpublished material, private messages and the identities of sources. Under K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, (2017) 10 SCC 1, any intrusion into privacy must be backed by law, necessary and proportionate. Making a journalist delete footage of police action destroys the record of how the police used their powers.

Further, on 5 October, the Delhi Police issued "Guidelines for journalists" asking reporters to carry identity cards issued by their organisations "and/or valid PIB/DIP accreditation cards". On 10 October, Newslaundry reported that police were asking media personnel whether they were YouTubers, refusing entry to those who were, and asking for PIB accreditation. Press cards however did not prevent detention and reporters from at least nine outlets were detained on 10 October, and from at least seven on 11 October. Digital journalist Pragya Mishra was detained in the RK Ashram area, and by her account her camera person was beaten even though both carried identification.

Detentions and the use of force are not ordinarily part of IFF's work given our focus on digital rights. We address them here because they affect the freedom of speech and expression of digital first journalists, who report and publish through their phones. Here we note, Article 19(1)(a) protects the freedom of the press (Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1985) 1 SCC 641), whether a journalist works for a newspaper or runs a YouTube channel. PIB accreditation has never been a condition for reporting from a public place. When the police check accreditation at a protest and detain those without it, they are illegally deciding who may report.

We note that on 11 October, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana of the Supreme Court heard a contempt petition alleging violation of the Court's order of 9 October on metro and train services, and a habeas corpus petition concerning the reported detention of about 7,000 people. The Court found a prima facie case and issued notice. Taking note of the Solicitor General's statement that internet services had been restored, it directed that that "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever." However, to our regret, there has been little compliance of this order as journalists were detained again that afternoon, a few hours after the order.
Our demands

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Government of NCT of Delhi and the Delhi Police to:

1) Return every phone taken from journalists, disclose the legal basis, seizure memo and Section 105 recording for each, and confirm whether any data was copied.
2) Instruct all personnel in writing that no one may be made to delete footage or stopped from recording police action, and preserve all body-camera footage.
3) Withdraw the advisory of 5 October to the extent that it makes accreditation a condition for reporting, and ensure that journalists and creators covering protests are not detained or obstructed.
4) Place before the Supreme Court on 13 October 2026 the names of all journalists detained, the grounds of detention and the time of release. We also support the press bodies' call for an inquiry, which should be independent, time-bound and cover the complaints made by women journalists.
5) IFF will track compliance before the hearing on 13 October 2026 and is examining legal remedies, including for the phones taken from journalists. 

Journalists and creators who were detained, had devices taken, were made to delete footage, or had posts or accounts restricted for covering the protests may write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. Even today, if they have to prove their loyalty to the country and the public, it is highly shameful.”

A 3-member Election Commission.
2 members put objections on record at least 14 times in 10 months.
Official word: every decision was "unanimous".

Here are the receipts on CEC Gyanesh Kumar. Every point is sourced in the reply below.

1. How he got the job
Feb 2025: the first CEC picked under the 2023 law that removed the Chief Justice from the selection panel. Panel: Modi, Amit Shah, Rahul Gandhi. Gandhi's dissent note asked them to wait for the Supreme Court. They didn't.

2. His previous boss
Secretary, Ministry of Cooperation, 2022 to Jan 2024. The minister: Amit Shah. Before that, a key Home Ministry officer on the 2019 Article 370 exercise.

3. The deletions
The SIR has cut about 13 crore names from voter rolls (AP, Reuters: 130 million+). The EC says these are dead, shifted or duplicate voters. In Bihar alone about 65 lakh were cut from the draft roll, and the Supreme Court had to order the EC to publish the names.

4. The "high-tech" software
Maharashtra's draft roll listed 2,70,313 voters as aged 101 to 150, because the system defaulted their birth year to 1900. It was fixed only after the state CEO flagged it.

5. The objections
Indian Express, Sept 23: Election Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi put objections on record at least 14 times in 10 months, four on a single day. One change was called "unauthorised and illegal". The EC's reply: decisions were "unanimous". It did not deny the notes exist.

6. The Form 6 claim
Sept 26: the EC said the Supreme Court had upheld its Form 6 declaration.
Oct 5: the CJI said in court that the SC had approved no modified Form 6.

7. Every exit locked
Mar-Apr: 193 MPs sign the first-ever notices to remove a CEC. Refused without detailed reasons.
Oct 5: the SC declines to suspend him and issues notice.
Oct 6: about 240 MPs march to the EC. Stopped by police.
Oct 10: 2,000+ detained in Delhi (Reuters, citing an MHA official).

text:
The battlefield doesn't check your follower count.

Every few weeks, Indian defence tech gets a new hero. A slick launch video. A funding headline. "Indigenous" in bold, "made in India" in the caption, and somewhere in the footnotes, an open-source stack, a white-labelled import, and a codebase an AI wrote over the weekend.

The applause is loud. The deployment orders are silent.

Let me be fair: open source is a great foundation, importing to learn is smart, and AI-assisted coding is a real superpower. None of these are the problem. The problem is when we confuse a demo with a capability, and visibility with viability.

A drone that flies beautifully in a Bengaluru tech park has passed exactly one test: the Bengaluru tech park. The real exams are harder:
→ Heavy electronic jamming
→ Desert dust, mountain cold, and coastal salt
→ A soldier with gloves on, no Wi-Fi, and zero patience
→ A foreign supplier who stops answering emails mid-conflict

You can't growth-hack your way through those.

Somewhere, there's a team without a PR agency, a podcast tour, or a viral reel. They've failed field trials, rebuilt the hardware twice, and own every line of their firmware. You haven't heard of them. Our forces probably will.

Before you celebrate the next defence "unicorn," ask:
1️⃣ Who has actually used it, and would they use it again?
Not a demo for officials, but a unit that ran it in jamming, dust, and cold, and still asked for more.

2️⃣ Remove every open-source module, imported part, and AI-generated line. What's left that's truly yours?
If the answer fits on one slide, that's not a product. It's packaging.

3️⃣ If a foreign supplier switched you off tonight, how many days could you keep delivering?
And how long would it take to replace them with an Indian source?

4️⃣ Which certifications and qualification standards have you cleared, and which are you "working towards"?
In defence, "working towards" usually means "not yet."

5️⃣ Who audits your code and firmware, and where does your data go?
In defence, "we trust our vendor" is the wrong answer.
If the answers are vague, the capability probably is too.

Reach gets you followers. Reliability gets you contracts.
Hype raises a round. Hardware wins a war.

Let's back the founders who build for the frontline, not the feed.

Ask harder questions. Build real things. Put the budget in R&D, not in reels.

My mother did not hesitate to bring up the circumstances around my birth and conception every time I tried her patience as a young boy. Granted, she always told me she loved me, but I got to know my chequered history quite early. “Your father’s parents owned a shop and the women who worked there assured me that it was unacceptable and totally reprehensible, a taboo, for an African woman and an Asian man to get together, let alone produce a child from that union. The only solution they said, was to perform an abortion and end that life before it even began. But I refused!" 

I was conceived towards the end of the 60s, a few years into Uganda’s journey as an independent country, a few years before Idi Amin Dada started his rule in Uganda. I am told it was the time of miniskirts and twist dancing in Uganda, and the time of the American sex revolution! My father was a young Asian of (most likely) Indian descent whose family was one of the trading families in Masaka. 

He was a student at Makerere University, and that is the extent of my knowledge about my father. Soon after I was born, President Iddi Amin declared an economic war of indigenization and my father was among those who were deported/expelled out of Uganda. The History of Uganda is such that Asians, particularly Indians took the lion’s share of trading licences. President Amin wanted to reverse this unfair advantage but unfortunately, it meant I would never get to meet my father or his family. Not only was I born in a conflicted relationship of races, I never got a chance to know who my father was, nor his family. Despite the great love and acceptance that I received from my mother, siblings and my Baganda tribal family, I always felt a great sense of “father hunger” - that yearning for fatherly protection, provision and affirmation which only a Dad could provide. 

My mother was a primary school teacher who was struggling to raise eight children as a single parent. She had been married to James Kyeyune, a medical officer and they were blessed with six children but their marriage broke down. My mother always told me that she could not accept being a co-wife. My step father had brought another wife home and she could not accept the idea of sharing a husband. Despite the efforts of the good catholic bishops who intervened to smooth things over, the marriage broke down and she moved away in the mid-60s to start a new life as a teacher and a single mother. I was born into a family of seven other children, five boys and two girls. Dickson, the eldest had gone off to join the police force, Joseph the second born and Edward the fifth born stayed with their paternal grandparents. Clare and Fred were students in a Catholic boarding school and came home only during the holidays. This meant that the three youngest children Florence, John and myself were the ones who stayed home with mother. 

Owing to my bi-racial parentage, my looks were quite different from the rest of the family and the children around me. I had big curly hair unlike my brother’s kinky hair. I had much lighter skin due to my father’s suspected Asian descent. In our Baganda culture, the name of a child is based on the clan of the father and in the absence of my biological father, my mother gave me the names of her father, Ssempa which meant that I belonged to my mother’s clan; symbolically represented by the colobus monkey (Nkima). My grandfather, Alipo Ssempa was an educated British colonial government administrator and interpreter in Masaka. Sadly, I never got to meet him as death took him before we could meet. His father, Bisakka or Bishaka who was my great grandfather had been a noteworthy regional trader in the Buganda, Ankole, Bunyoro, Rwanda and Tanzania region. 

He was called Bisaka, a name very closely related to Kisaka which is a large cluster or collection of trees and bushes which occurs on the savannah plains and hills in this region. It’s like an individual collection of a family of trees and bushes which are separated from others by savannah grass fields. Just as his name implies, my great grandfather had eighty wives which made up his large family! Bisaka was known as Bishaka by the western Ankole-Rwanda tribes whose language is characterized by the ‘sh’ making him multi tribal/multi lingual and multi-wifey. Unfortunately, this great trader and lover of the sweet affections of the beautiful women of Buganda, Ankole, Rwanda and Tanzania region suffered an early death which led to the scattering of the whole family. 

My great grandmother "Venecka Munaku Atambuza Mwoyo" [the poor walks guided by the spirit] and her sister who had also been a co-wife branched out Eastward and settled between Mityebiri/ Minziro in Rakai and Buyikuzi in Lukaya which is half way between Kampala city and Masaka town. Thus I carried the genes of Bisaka and the name of his son Ssempa, a fact which made people do a double take every time they met the bi-racial child with a native African name. It was not the norm. 

These bio-genetical differences were much more pronounced in my childhood. I stuck out both in the classroom and on the children’s playfield. I can compare it to being the only black student in an all-white students school or being the only white student at an all-black-African students school. To some, I was an object of curiosity and I often had to bear the discomfort of having my hair felt, so the kids with kinky hair could feel my curly hair. Most of them were kind, but others would mock me with unkind words, ”Ssempa was forgotten at the airport, the Indians forgot him with the suitcases and boxes at the airport.” They would laugh and others gave me the monicker, ‘Magoba ga Uganda’ a Luganda phrase meaning “Ugandan profit” which they would explain with youthful logic; “In the interaction between Uganda and India, Ssempa was the Ugandan profit.” These were painful words casually thrown around by some misguided youngsters. They did not reflect the sentiment of the whole Buganda community which accepted me as a son. But in the places where children interacted with minimal adult supervision; the classrooms, playing fields where adults were absent to guide, I was often called painful names, like ‘illegitimate,’ ‘bastard,’ ‘magoba ga Uganda.’ It is a fact of life that some children will mock those who are different or handicapped, maybe they have unusually large ears or nose. This is the foolishness of childhood which fortunately disappears as we grow older. 

Narozali is found in Buyange Parish, Kyanamukakaaka subcounty in Masaka district in the South West of Uganda. It was a large Roman catholic parish with a church, schools and many other projects run by the church. It was located about one hour from Masaka town, on the undulating hills surrounding the shores of Lake Victoria. My mother was a grade one (primary one) teacher at the parish and we stayed in a house provided by the school. My mother was a devout catholic and we attended daily morning mass as well as family evening prayers. We prayed much when there was trouble such as when there was war in the period of 1971-72. In 1971, the president of Uganda, Apollo Milton Obote was overthrown by his star General, Idi Amin Dada in a military takeover that changed Uganda’s political and economic terrain in which I was to grow up. First, the expulsion of Asians in his economic war policy of indigenization was a strange mixture of tragedy and triumph. It was tragic to the Indians whose families had built and run the back bone of the Ugandan economy and were unceremoniously expelled from the country. Most of all the industries, commercial farms, large and small trading shops were owned and run by Indian families who had the technical skills, experience and passion to operate them effectively. They were forced to vacate all of this in a short time not knowing where they were to go. The sudden loss of homes and wealth which had been accumulated for nearly a century led some unfortunate souls to suicides by the river Nile. Others travelled to Canada, England, Kenya and United States where they started a new life. Some ended up succeeding incredibly in their new homes, becoming the economic entrepreneurs of their new homelands. Soon after Idi Amin became president of Uganda, there was an ill-fated attempt to attack and militarily overthrow him by rebels based out of Tanzania. 

Our home of Narozali is in the South West region of Uganda’s territory next to Tanzania and at times, it seemed that we were living in a war zone. Military vehicles, jeeps and noisy Israeli-made warplanes above made it difficult to ignore the ongoing conflict. We spent a lot of time praying to God to intervene and even added special supplications to the Virgin Mary who had a special altar with her monument encased in a specially made grotto. Here we earnestly recited the rosary and asked for divine intervention. Providentially, the war ended soon as the attackers were defeated in a bloody massacre! The early efforts by the coalition of anti-Idi Amini forces to remove him militarily were unsuccessful and suffered huge casualties. For the natives, it was also a mixture of triumph and tragedy. Their struggle for independence from colonial masters had given them political gains without economic gains. The economy was controlled by the Indian merchant families giving little or no space for the emergence of African owned enterprises. This all changed suddenly as Iddi Amin began to apportion out enterprises to the natives. My mother applied to operate a stone quarry but was denied for some reason. However, native Ugandan's got to own and operate all sorts of businesses from industries to merchant shops. While it is true that many ended up being mismanaged and run into the ground, there were others which succeeded. The expulsion of the Asians/ Indians created a leadership vacuum which forced many Ugandans to quickly learn to trade in various enterprises, giving rise to Ugandan owned business. 

As a child of dual Asian-Ugandan ancestry, it was a loss for my father’s people, and a gain for my mother’s people. As Nyinamwiru, the daughter of Bukuku lamented when she learnt that her father had been killed by her son Karabumbi Nduhura who was now the new king, “My ears cause me to hear both evil and good, for is it not my son who has killed Bukuku? My father is dead, but my son reigns, thus I have sorrow on one arm but joy on the other.” This historical account of our ancestors’ dilemma describes my conflicted view of Idi Amin’s expulsion of Indians from Uganda. This view was later to be articulated in my college days by a professor of Political Science at Makerere University who said that Amin’s expulsion of Indians was the single most significant event in economic empowerment of the Ugandan natives. It was quite interesting because, Professor Mahmood Mamdani, was a Ugandan with Asian ancestry, just like me. To date, Uganda, unlike its East African counterparts Kenya and Tanzania has the greatest number of Africans who own business while the other two have businesses still largely owned by the original Asian families who had no Iddi Amin to shake them up. 

Excerpts from "Magoba Ga Uganda" the Auto Biography of Pastor Martin Ssempa..now Coming out later in Dec 2025

THE LAST BENEFICIARY
EPISODE 2 — THE WOMAN AT THE DOOR
COMPLETE READER’S VERSION

CHAPTER 1 — THE FAMILY CALL

My son had signed a form identifying my body.
Now his uncle was calling to ask whether I’d seen it.
I picked up the phone outside the school and started recording.
“Put Daniel on.”
“Nora. Take Ben home.”
“You booked my funeral.”
He went quiet.
The woman in the beige coat reached for my phone. I stepped away.
“Speak to your wife,” his brother said.
Daniel’s voice came through.
“Do what he says.”
I asked him where Ben had broken his arm when he was nine.
“The playground behind your mother’s.”
Right answer. Wrong instruction.

CHAPTER 2 — THE OTHER FUNERAL

I took Ben back through the school gate. The woman followed us.
In reception, I told the secretary we’d been threatened. She locked the outer door and called the police.
The woman put her phone on the desk.
“He’ll move Daniel when they come.”
“Who did I bury?” I asked.
She looked at Ben.
I turned him toward me.
“Nobody gets to make you answer for them.”
The woman opened a photograph.
A man on a beach. Broad shoulders. Daniel’s height. A different face.
“My husband,” she said.
“You collected Daniel’s death money.”
“Your brother-in-law told me it was payment for keeping quiet.”
Ben sat down hard.

CHAPTER 3 — THE MESSAGE HE DELETED

“You knew?” I asked him.
“Only that Dad was alive. Uncle said you were the reason he couldn’t come back.”
He handed me his phone.
The identification form was there in a message. Sign, or your father dies.
“He made me delete the video.”
It was still in the deleted folder.
I restored it.
Daniel sat in the same chair. His brother stood behind him.
The woman went white when she saw the full recording.
“That’s not the one he sent me.”
On screen, Daniel leaned forward.
“Ben. I agreed to the money. I never agreed to your mother.”
His brother’s hand settled on his shoulder.
“Then you should have stayed dead.”

CHAPTER 4 — THE WOMAN AT THE DOOR

Outside reception, a uniformed officer tried the locked door.
The secretary reached for the release.
I held up my hand.
On Ben’s phone, the video kept playing.
Someone entered behind Daniel’s brother.
A woman in police uniform.
She took the funeral receipt from his hand.
“Get the boy’s signature,” she said. “I’ll handle Nora.”
The officer outside tapped the glass.
Same face. Same crooked little smile.
“Nora Vale? Your son called us.”
Ben shook his head.
The secretary still had the police on the line.
“She’s here already,” she said into the receiver.
Then she looked at me.
“They say they haven’t sent anyone yet.”

Original fiction by Night Shift Confessions.

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
RAHUL GANDHI REMOVED FROM AKASHVANI BHAVAN: A PROTEST THAT COULD NOT BE ENDED BY BARRICADES

What happened at Akashvani Bhavan on 6 October deserves to be examined beyond the political slogans.

After opposition MPs were stopped from marching towards the Election Commission, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and other leaders staged a sit-in inside the Akashvani Bhavan premises. The protest continued for nearly nine hours before Delhi Police moved in and detained them. 

The source video records Rahul Gandhi repeatedly asking the police a remarkably simple question:

“Tell me where I can sit. If there is another place where I can peacefully protest, I will go there.” 

That is the question that should concern every democracy.

If a protest is creating a genuine public inconvenience, authorities have the legitimate responsibility to regulate it. But regulation should also provide a clear, lawful and practical alternative for peaceful assembly.

Rahul Gandhi and the Opposition said they wanted to reach the Election Commission to meet the commissioners and raise their objections concerning SIR and electoral rolls. The Election Commission, however, subsequently said that it had received no formal meeting request from any political party—an important point that must also be addressed honestly. 

So there are questions for both sides:

To the protesters: Was a formal request for a meeting actually submitted, and were lawful protest conditions followed?

To the authorities: If the march could not proceed, where exactly were the elected representatives permitted to conduct their peaceful protest?

To the Election Commission: Why not create a transparent channel for elected representatives to present their documented concerns and receive an institutional response?

The allegations of “vote theft” and electoral manipulation remain political allegations and must be established through evidence and constitutional process. But the underlying questions about voter rolls, SIR and electoral transparency deserve answers—not dismissal.

Today, the confrontation has moved beyond one march.

The real test is whether India's democratic institutions can absorb dissent without treating dissent itself as the problem.

Barricades can stop a march.
Detention can end a sit-in.
Neither can substitute for an answer.

Democracy ultimately demands something stronger than silence: credible institutions, transparent processes and the freedom to question power peacefully.

text:
INDIA TELLS THE UN THAT ITS DEMOCRACY PROTECTS FREE MEDIA AND PEACEFUL PROTEST—BUT DO THE FACTS ON THE GROUND MATCH THAT CLAIM?

Garima Singh of Desh Ki Garima raises a serious contradiction that every citizen should examine.

India’s response to the United Nations human rights office defended the country’s democratic institutions, independent judiciary, free media and constitutional protection for peaceful assembly. Yet, during the recent Delhi protests, journalists and protesters reported detention, rough handling and the seizure of recording equipment.

According to the video, journalist Anil Shukla’s camera was seized by people alleged to be Delhi Police personnel and was not returned. This specific allegation demands verification and an official explanation.

THE QUESTION IS SIMPLE: IF INDIA’S INSTITUTIONS PROTECT PRESS FREEDOM, WHY ARE JOURNALISTS REPORTING THAT THEY WERE PREVENTED FROM DOING THEIR JOB?

This is not merely a political argument. On 10 October, the United Nations human rights office expressed concern over reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, civil-society members, lawyers and journalists. On 11 October, India rejected those concerns as unwarranted interference in its internal affairs.

Human Rights Watch, in its statement dated 13 October 2026, also reported allegations of excessive force, arbitrary detention and the seizure of journalists’ phones and equipment during the protests. These reports call for transparent investigation and accountability—not blanket dismissal or uncritical acceptance of every allegation.

A DEMOCRACY MUST BE JUDGED BY ITS CONDUCT, NOT ONLY BY ITS OFFICIAL STATEMENTS.

The Constitution protects freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms under Article 19(1)(b), subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions.

Police may enforce lawful restrictions, but journalists must not be obstructed or have their equipment unlawfully seized merely because they document events that authorities find uncomfortable. Any seizure or detention must have a lawful basis and remain open to scrutiny.

We demand:

• A transparent account of every journalist detained during the protests.

• An explanation of the reported seizure of Anil Shukla’s camera, including its present whereabouts and the legal grounds for the action.

• An independent investigation into allegations of assault, intimidation and obstruction of journalists.

• Accountability wherever misconduct is established.

• Respect for peaceful protest, press freedom and the constitutional rights of every citizen.

India cannot claim democratic credibility internationally while leaving credible allegations of violations at home unanswered. Patriotism does not mean shielding institutions from scrutiny. It means demanding that they honour the Constitution.

LET THE FACTS BE EXAMINED. LET THE PRESS REPORT FREELY. LET PEACEFUL CITIZENS EXERCISE THEIR CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS.

text:
Somewhere in 1945, at the dead of the night, the British intelligence intercepted a suspicious-looking seagoing trawler near the coast of Mumbai. A team of police raided the trawler but could find only kitchen utensils and gunny bags. The trawler was travelling from Yangon in Myanmar and the cargo belonged to a Gujarati engineer, B. C. Mehta. As soon as the trawler reached the coast Mehta took all the bags and utensils with him and went straight to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Why would a man coming from Yangon take those insignificant utensils and gunny bags to one of the tallest leaders of the Indian freedom struggle? 

Mehta was, in fact, on a very important mission. The mission was to tell the tales of bravery of valour displayed by Azad Hind Fauj on the battle field. Those gunny bags were hiding reels of a documentary film made by the propaganda unit of Fauj.

When Fauj led by Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose started suffering reverses in the war it was felt that Indians living in India needed to know the real story of Netaji. The British government had put severe censors on any news of Azad Hind Fauj. Indians were fed with a narrative that Netaji was a Japanese agent and Fauj was nothing but the Indian Japanese Fighting Force formed to establish Japanese colonialism in India. Though Fauj had a propaganda unit, its penetration into the Indian mainland was not much.

The propaganda unit of Fauj on the orders of Netaji made a documentary film that showed Netaji, soldiers on the battlefield, Rani Jhansi regiment, and other engagements of Fauj. Netaji might have left India after bitter differences with Mahatma Gandhi but he still had his sympathizers and allies in the Indian National Congress. These pro-Netaji leaders were contacted so that the film could be shown to the Indian public.

Mehta was a Gujarati engineer belonging to a business family who would, several times, drive Netaji in his vehicle in Myanmar. Sardar Patel was contacted by Azad Hind Fauj regarding this film. He pledged his support to smuggle the film into India and Mehta was given the responsibility to bring it into Indian territory.

Sardar Patel took the reels of the film with him and rushed to New Delhi. The film needed to be watched by all the senior Congress leaders. Patel asked Congress activists to arrange for a public screening of the film. Rajeshwar Dayal, owner of Regal Cinema at Connaught Place, was requested to allow screening at his theatre. He agreed and screening was arranged.

On the scheduled day Sardar Patel, Jawahar Lal Nehru, Maulana Azad, and each of the members of the Congress High Command watched the film. The outlook towards Azad Hind Fauj and Netaji was changed. People realized that Netaji was on a national mission to free his motherland and evil propaganda of the British that he was a Japanese agent was a lie. Gautam Kaul writes, “The film showed sequences of the members of Azad Hind Fauj training in the jungle and also the work of Rani of Jhansi Brigade of Indian women based in Yangon and Singapore. It also featured Bose moving around on inspection and meeting with other leaders of the region as well as exhorting his workers to prepare themselves for a long march to Delhi.”

After the screening, as expected, Dayal received a notice from the government for violating the law. Rajinder Narain, who also argued at the famous Red Fort INA trials, was asked by Dayal to help him. Narain took him to Kunwar Mohinder Singh Bedi, who was the city magistrate then, and asked for his help. Bedi knew how to help a patriot within the ambit of colonial law. After the first hearing, he declared a long vacation. He did not list the case for hearings until India got independence. 

On the other hand, Sardar Patel asked his loyalists to arrange for more material on Netaji. He wanted a complete feature film on the great son of India. In 1947, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was released. The film was produced by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, directed by

TO INDIA’S ARMED FORCES AND POLICE: STAND WITH THE CONSTITUTION, PROTECT DEMOCRACY, CHOOSE HUMANITY

Credit: Video creator — Wg Cdr Anuma Aacharya

India’s freedom was won through immense sacrifice by those who stood against colonial oppression. The stories of our freedom fighters taught generations to value liberty, dignity and justice.

Today, nearly eight decades after Independence, the challenge is to preserve the democracy and Constitution for which those sacrifices continue to inspire us.

In this powerful appeal, Wg Cdr Anuma Aacharya reminds members of India’s armed forces and police that they are custodians of democratic values. She expresses concern about the fairness of elections and the protests arising from those concerns, urging security personnel not to use violence against their fellow citizens.

Her message is both moral and constitutional:

YOUR UNIFORM IS A RESPONSIBILITY, NOT A LICENCE TO HARM.

Members of the security forces deserve respect for their service. That respect must go hand in hand with accountability, restraint and fidelity to the Constitution.

When citizens raise concerns about electoral fairness, their allegations deserve impartial examination. Peaceful dissent must not be treated as a crime merely because it challenges those in power. Any restriction on protest or use of force must have a lawful basis and comply with applicable constitutional protections.

Remember: the Constitution is not the property of any political party or government. It is the framework that binds public power and protects the rights and dignity of every citizen.

Wg Cdr Anuma Aacharya’s appeal asks every person entrusted with state power to remember the human being behind every order.

An unlawful order does not become just because it comes from a superior. Every public servant has a duty to act within the law, protect life and dignity, and refuse unlawful violence.

The consequences of our choices may be remembered by future generations. History honours those who protect human dignity, not those who abandon it when obedience becomes easier than conscience.

WHEN THE MOMENT COMES, CHOOSE HUMANITY.

Stand with the Constitution. Protect peaceful protesters. Respect the right to dissent. Demand free and fair elections. Insist on independent investigations into allegations of wrongdoing, and ensure accountability wherever violations are established.

THE TRUE HONOUR OF A UNIFORM LIES IN PROTECTING THE PEOPLE, NOT IN MAKING THEM AFRAID.

Democracy survives when citizens speak freely and those entrusted with power remember that their first duty is to the Constitution and the people of India.
